extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; students of literature and moral philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of selected chapters from Montaigne's Essays (early modern philosophical/ethical reflections). Contains aphoristic moral criteria and examples rather than an explicit procedural rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in victory / conduct in war
rubrics_metrics.description: Victory is praiseworthy whether obtained by valour or wisdom, but it is dishonourable to obtain it by treachery or by taking unfair advantage of an opponent (e.g., assaulting during parley or by night).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Chrysippus and Alexander's refusal to attack Darius under cover of night: one should 'run as fast as they can' in contest but not 'lay any hand upon their adversary to stop him' or use stratagems to steal victory. Examples: betrayals at Genoa and Ligny are given as condemnable; the honourable man prefers to complain of ill-fortune than be ashamed of victory ('Malo me fortunae poeniteat, quam victoria pudeat'). Anti-patterns: attacking during parley, stealthy night executions, and treacherous stratagems.

rubrics_metrics.name: That the intention is judge of our actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral appraisal of an action should primarily consider the agent's intention and will, since effect and performance are often beyond our control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne discusses cases (Henry VII arranging a posthumous murder; Count Egmont seeking to have his execution free him from obligations) to show that we are masters only of our will and that obligations cannot be demanded beyond one's ability. Guidance: distinguish deliberate, premeditated breaches of faith (not excused) from failures arising from inability; penitence and intention matter morally even when outcomes differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt restitution — do not defer making amends
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to make amends only by will or after death is morally inadequate; restitution should be timely and burdensome to be truly meritorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne notes people who, convicted by conscience, postpone restitution to their wills after death — this is ineffective and often morally worse. The more costly and immediate the restitution, the more just and meritorious it is. Anti-pattern: deferring reparations to one’s last will or letting hatred persist to the 'last gasp.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding idleness — cultivate the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: An idle mind, left without applied study or aim, runs into unprofitable fantasies and wild imaginations; the mind must be cultivated and directed to productive pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne compares untended grounds producing weeds to minds that, without restraint, create 'chimaeras and fantastic monsters.' He advises preparation and cultivation of the mind for proper 'seeds' (studies) to prevent trivial or harmful reveries. Example: his own retirement intended for leisure produced roaming fancies he began to write down. Anti-pattern: excessive leisure that leaves the soul aimless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of lying; truth as social bond
rubrics_metrics.description: Lying is an accursed vice that undermines the social tie constituted by the word; it should be corrected severely from infancy because it is difficult to cure once habitual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne differentiates between untruth (mistaken statement) and lie (knowing falsehood) and focuses on the latter. He argues liars either invent or distort facts and will often contradict themselves; memory problems make lying risky. He gives diplomatic examples where falsehood trips up ambassadors. Parents should punish lying strictly; anti-patterns include tailoring speech to please powerful people, adapting stories differently to different audiences, and taking pride in 'the art' of lying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match speaking tempo to role; value of extempore wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Different speaking styles suit different roles: the slow, deliberate speaker better fits the pulpit; the quick, extempore speaker better fits the bar where rapid replies are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne suggests that over-elaboration can make speech stiff ('stink of oil and of the lamp') and that occasion, interruption, and suddenness often bring out wit. Examples: a lawyer (Monsieur de Poyet) who overprepared failed when circumstances changed; Severus Cassius spoke best extempore. Guidance: prefer extempore responses in adversarial contexts; avoid excessive premeditation that impedes spontaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about prognostication and divination
rubrics_metrics.description: Prognostics (oracles, augury, divination from stars, dreams, entrails) are unreliable and have lost most of their credit; one should not regulate important affairs by such vanities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recounts the decline of oracles, the multiplicity of false prognostics and the incidental hits that gain undue attention. Examples include princes misled by astrological/prophetic reports (Francesco of Saluzzo). He notes cultural practices that leave many false predictions unrecorded and the seductiveness of ambiguous prophetic language. Anti-patterns: making political or personal decisions based on almanacs, ambiguous prophecies, or superstitious auguries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy: resolution and brave endurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Constancy involves bravely facing and stoutly suffering those inconveniences which cannot be avoided, while still taking honest and decent means to prevent harms when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne clarifies that constancy does not forbid fear or prudent efforts to avoid mischiefs; rather, it commends steadfast endurance of unavoidable adversity. Guidance: employ all decent means to secure oneself, but when harm is inescapable, bear it with fortitude.
